# Internal audit and management review

**GENERATED by tools/generate_internal_audit.py — do not edit.**
Regenerate with `make docs`; `tests/test_internal_audit.py` fails if the
committed file and the generator disagree.

C9, OR-5. ISO/IEC 27001 clauses 9.2, 9.3 and 10.2; SOC 2 CC4.1 and CC4.2.

## The practice exists; the cycle does not

The pre-production review recorded **151 findings**:
a control examined, what was actually true, and the change that keeps it fixed.
That is clause 10.2 — nonconformity and corrective action — in the shape the
clause asks for, written before anybody thought to call it that. An auditor
asking to see corrective actions can be handed that log, on request; it is not
published, and [REVIEW_FINDINGS.md](REVIEW_FINDINGS.md) indexes it here.

What does not exist is a **cycle**: a schedule, an owner, a scope agreed in
advance, and minutes signed afterwards. That is OR-5, and no repository can
produce it. This document is the programme those meetings would follow.

## Impartiality, which cannot be satisfied here

Clause 9.2.2 requires auditors selected so as to ensure objectivity, and says
auditors shall not audit their own work.

**One person cannot do that.** In an organisation of this size the person
auditing a control is the person who built it, and every finding in the review
log was found by its author. Saying so is the only honest option: the
alternative is a programme that implies an independence it does not have, which
an auditor will find in the first interview.

What partly substitutes, and does not fully: the evidence for a `Verified` row
is a test somebody else can run, and a reviewer who runs it is not taking the
author's word. That is reproducibility rather than independence. Where the
organisation grows, or a contractor can be used for a cycle, the gap closes.

## Method, by status

Clause 9.2.1 asks a programme to consider the importance of what is audited and
the results of previous audits. The register already encodes both: a status is
the conclusion of the last examination, and it determines what evidence exists
to re-examine. So the method is derived from it, and the order is too — what
nobody has proven comes before what a test proves on every commit.

### 1. `Process` — 7 rows

**What the auditor does.** Ask the accountable person for the record — the signature, the completed training, the minutes, the contract. The evidence for these rows is not in this repository and cannot be; the audit is the act of asking.

**What is a finding.** There is no record, or nobody is accountable. Both are nonconformities against clause 9.2, and the second is the more serious.

### 2. `Partial` — 2 rows

**What the auditor does.** Establish what the missing half is, and whether it has moved since the last audit. The row states it; the audit is checking that the statement is still the true one rather than the one written when somebody last looked.

**What is a finding.** The missing half is not what the row says it is, in either direction — it has been built and the row still claims a gap, or it has grown and the row does not.

### 3. `Operator` — 3 rows

**What the auditor does.** Audit the documentation, not the control. These are controls a customer operates — TLS termination, disk encryption, backups of their database — so the only thing auditable here is whether what we tell them is accurate and complete.

**What is a finding.** The instruction to the operator is missing, wrong, or describes something the software no longer does.

### 4. `Verified` — 41 rows

**What the auditor does.** Run the evidence. Each of these cites a test, a demonstration or a measurement; the audit is executing it and then asking the harder question — **does it still measure what it claims?** A guard that has silently stopped checking anything passes exactly like one that works.

**What is a finding.** The evidence no longer runs, no longer exists, or passes for a reason other than the control working. R-10 is that failure and it has been found repeatedly here.

## Management review inputs

Clause 9.3.2 lists what a management review must consider. Most of it already
exists here as a generated document, so the agenda points at files rather than
asking somebody to assemble a pack — and a test fails if any cited file stops
existing.

| Clause | Input | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|
| 9.3.2 a) | The status of actions from previous management reviews | **Nothing yet** — see below |
| 9.3.2 b) | Changes in external and internal issues relevant to the ISMS | `docs/DECISIONS.md` |
| 9.3.2 c) 1) | Nonconformities and corrective actions | `docs/REVIEW_FINDINGS.md` |
| 9.3.2 c) 2) | Monitoring and measurement results | `charts/igni/files/alerts.yaml` |
| 9.3.2 c) 3) | Audit results | **Nothing yet** — see below |
| 9.3.2 c) 4) | Fulfilment of information security objectives | `docs/COMPLIANCE_TRACKER.md` |
| 9.3.2 d) | Feedback from interested parties | **Nothing yet** — see below |
| 9.3.2 e) | Results of risk assessment and status of the risk treatment plan | `docs/RISK_ASSESSMENT.md` |
| 9.3.2 f) | Opportunities for continual improvement | `docs/COMPLIANCE_TRACKER.md` |

**9.3.2 a), the status of actions from previous management reviews.** There have been no previous management reviews, so there are no actions to carry forward. This is the first cycle and the input is empty for a reason that will stop being true after one meeting.

**9.3.2 c) 3), audit results.** No internal audit has been conducted under a programme. The examinations recorded in the pre-production review (`docs/REVIEW_FINDINGS.md`) are audit work in substance — a control examined, a finding, a corrective action — but they were not conducted against a programme, by an independent auditor, or to a schedule, so calling them audit results would be claiming a form that was not followed.

**9.3.2 d), feedback from interested parties.** There are no customers yet, so there is no feedback. Recorded rather than omitted, because an empty input a reader can see is different from one that was never considered.

## The cycle, which a person has to set

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Organisation | `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` |
| Audit programme owner | `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` |
| Internal audit frequency | `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` |
| Management review frequency | `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` |
| Next internal audit due | `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` |
| Next management review due | `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` |
| Where minutes are kept | `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` |
| Approved by | `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` |
| Date of approval | `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` |

Minutes are the output an auditor asks for, and the one thing this document
cannot produce even in draft: a decision nobody made cannot be recorded. What
a set should contain is who attended, which revision of this programme was
followed, what was examined, what was found, and what was decided — with an
owner and a date against each decision, because clause 9.3.2 a) makes those the
first input to the next review.

## What this document is not

**Evidence that an audit happened.** It says what to examine and how. Nothing
here asserts that anybody did, and no field above is filled in.

**A substitute for the review log.** The review log is where findings
live, and it should stay that way — a second place to record them is how two
records of the same thing start disagreeing.

**Applicable to the certification audit.** That is OR-7 and C10: a different
activity, done by somebody else, needing a contract and an observation window.
